nodes.content: Design an embedded runtime that contains peripheral-driver faults while preserving hard real-time deadlines and safe shared-device recovery.
requirements: Under driver crashes, hangs, and invalid DMA requests, protected control tasks retain 1 ms deadlines.
Recover shared-device service within 50 ms without stale DMA writes or cross-partition state corruption.

nodes.content: Reserve controls a dedicated core; sandbox drivers with IOMMU DMA domains and recover shared devices via revoke–drain–reset–epoch fencing.
Can IOMMU revocation and drain–reset–epoch fencing block stale DMA after driver crashes within the 50 ms recovery budget?
Device reset, DMA drain, IOTLB invalidation, and epoch-fenced remapping prevent stale writes and restore service within 50 ms.
Run DMA-FenceBench: inject crashes with outstanding DMA across 10,000 resets; measure stale writes and shared-device recovery latency.
DMA-FenceBench observed zero stale writes across 10,000 resets; worst-case shared-device recovery was 43 ms.
Adopt drain–reset–epoch fencing for shared-device recovery: DMA-FenceBench found zero stale writes and 43 ms worst-case restoration.
After adopting drain–reset–epoch fencing, implement dedicated-core scheduling and IOMMU isolation; inject driver faults against 1-ms deadlines and 50-ms recovery.
Run RT-FaultBench across 100,000 control releases, injecting crashes, hangs, and invalid DMA; measure misses, recovery latency, and isolation breaches.
RT-FaultBench report with timestamped control-release traces, injected-fault logs, DMA-isolation checks, and shared-device recovery-latency histograms.
Audit RT-FaultBench report traces for 1-ms deadline misses, stale DMA writes, partition corruption, and recovery exceeding 50 ms.
RT-FaultBench measured 68 ms recovery after a driver hang, exceeding the 50 ms limit despite crash-only recovery reaching 43 ms.
Use 5-ms hang detection, bounded DMA fencing with device-reset escalation, then IOTLB invalidation and epoch-gated remapping.
The shared device stops all DMA within 10 ms of an independent hardware reset, even when its driver hangs.
Replay RT-FaultBench’s logged hang 10,000 times; assert independent reset and measure last DMA transaction latency against 10 ms.
Across 10,000 hang replays, 37 independent resets allowed DMA past 10 ms; worst last-DMA latency was 18 ms.
Allowing 20 ms for hardware-confirmed DMA quiescence after reset prevents stale writes while keeping hang recovery below 50 ms.
Replay RT-FaultBench hangs across 10,000 resets; require hardware-confirmed DMA quiescence within 20 ms, then measure stale writes and recovery.
Across 10,000 hang replays, DMA quiesced within 19 ms with zero stale writes, but recovery reached 54 ms.
Using RT-FaultBench fault logs, profile detection, reset, quiescence, and remapping during hang replays against the 50-ms recovery limit.
Hang profiles found 11 ms serialized shadow-map preparation; overlapping it with quiescence projects 43 ms recovery from 54 ms.
Overlapping shadow-map preparation with confirmed DMA quiescence, then IOTLB invalidation and epoch-gated remapping, achieves ≤50-ms recovery without stale writes.
Replay RT-FaultBench logs with overlapped shadow-map preparation, IOTLB invalidation, and epoch-gated remapping; measure 10,000 hang recoveries and stale writes.
Across 10,000 hang replays, overlapped shadow-map preparation cut worst recovery to 44 ms, with zero stale DMA writes.
Reserve a control core; IOMMU-sandbox drivers, overlap post-reset DMA quiescence with shadow-map preparation, then invalidate IOTLB and epoch-gate remapping.
Do reserved-core scheduling and per-driver IOMMU domains prevent 1-ms deadline misses and cross-partition corruption during invalid DMA requests?
Dedicated control-core scheduling and per-driver IOMMU domains yield zero 1-ms deadline misses and zero cross-partition writes under injected driver faults.
Run RT-IsolationBench across 1,000,000 control releases with driver crashes, hangs, and illegal DMA; record deadline misses and cross-partition writes.
Across 1,000,000 releases, RT-IsolationBench recorded six 1-ms deadline misses during IOTLB invalidation; zero cross-partition writes.
Prioritize control traffic with fabric QoS and bound IOTLB invalidation bursts to 20 µs; retain overlapped, epoch-gated recovery.
Implement fabric QoS and bounded invalidations; rerun fault injection to check 1-ms deadlines, partition isolation, and ≤50-ms recovery.
Configure control-core fabric priority and 20-µs IOTLB invalidation bursts; rerun RT-IsolationBench and 10,000 hang recoveries.
QoS-FenceBench report containing deadline traces, fabric-priority settings, IOTLB burst durations, isolation checks, and 10,000 recovery latencies.
Audit QoS-FenceBench traces for deadline misses, cross-partition writes, invalidation bursts over 20 µs, and recovery beyond 50 ms.
QoS-FenceBench found zero deadline misses in 1,000,000 releases, zero cross-partition writes, and 47 ms worst-case recovery.
Replay QoS-FenceBench’s worst recovery trace under concurrent DMA faults and bus saturation; check deadlines, stale writes, and restoration latency.
Under concurrent DMA faults and bus saturation, worst-case recovery rose to 56 ms; deadlines and DMA isolation held.
Retain fabric QoS and bounded IOTLB invalidations for deadlines; defer recovery-policy adoption because saturated-bus recovery reaches 56 ms.
Guarantee 15% fabric bandwidth for recovery below protected-control priority; retain IOMMU isolation, 20-µs invalidation bursts, and overlapped epoch-gated remapping.
Does a 15% recovery-bandwidth reservation restore saturated-bus service within 50 ms without missing 1-ms deadlines or allowing stale DMA?
With overlapped epoch-gated remapping, 15% recovery bandwidth yields ≤50-ms saturated-bus recovery, zero stale writes, and zero 1-ms deadline misses.
Replay RT-FaultBench logs across 10,000 saturated-bus runs with 15% reserved bandwidth and overlapped epoch fencing; measure deadlines, stale writes, recovery.
Across 10,000 saturated-bus runs, worst recovery was 49 ms, with zero stale writes and zero 1-ms deadline misses.
Replay RT-FaultBench’s simultaneous hang and invalid-DMA traces under saturated-bus bursts; measure recovery tails, control deadlines, and cross-partition writes.
Simultaneous hangs and invalid DMA under saturated bursts produced 53 ms worst-case recovery; no deadline misses or cross-partition writes occurred.
With 15% bandwidth, prioritize reset over invalid-DMA logging while overlapping epoch-gated remapping; predict ≤50-ms recovery without stale writes or misses.
Replay RT-FaultBench concurrent hang/invalid-DMA traces under saturation, prioritizing reset over logging; measure recovery, stale writes, and deadline misses.
Reset-first replay reduced worst concurrent-fault recovery from 53 to 48 ms; zero stale writes and 1-ms deadline misses.
Adopt reset-first recovery with 15% bandwidth: concurrent-fault recovery fell from 53 to 48 ms without stale writes or misses.
Implement adopted reset-first recovery with 15% reserved bandwidth, then certify 1-ms deadlines, DMA isolation, and ≤50-ms service restoration.
Implement reset-first handler with 5-ms watchdog, 15% recovery bandwidth, hardware-confirmed DMA quiescence, 20-µs IOTLB bursts, and epoch-gated remapping.
Recovery Runtime v0.9: reset-first watchdog handler, 15% fabric reservation, bounded IOTLB invalidation, and epoch-fenced DMA remapping.
Stress-test Recovery Runtime v0.9 with crashes, hangs, invalid DMA, and saturated buses; record deadlines, stale writes, and recovery.
Recovery Runtime v0.9 stress tests recorded zero deadline misses or stale writes; worst saturated-bus restoration was 49 ms.
Run a 24-hour hardware-in-loop reset/DMA boundary-timing campaign on Recovery Runtime v0.9; log recovery tails, deadline misses, and cross-partition writes.
The 24-hour hardware-in-loop campaign found one lost reset-completion interrupt causing 52 ms recovery; no deadline misses or cross-partition writes.
Recovery-core 250-µs reset-status polling should bypass lost interrupts, preserving confirmed DMA quiescence, ≤50-ms recovery, and 1-ms deadlines.
Replay RT-FaultBench traces with suppressed reset interrupts and 250-µs recovery-core polling; measure quiescence, stale writes, deadlines, and restoration latency.
Across 10,000 suppressed-interrupt replays, polling confirmed DMA quiescence; worst recovery was 49 ms, with zero stale writes or deadline misses.
Adopt reset-first recovery with 250-µs polling and 15% bandwidth; lost-interrupt recovery fell from 52 to 49 ms without stale writes.
Add 250-µs recovery-core reset polling to Runtime v0.9, then recertify deadline isolation, DMA fencing, and ≤50-ms restoration.
Patch Recovery Runtime v0.9 with 250-µs reset-status polling on the recovery core; retain interrupt handling and hardware-confirmed DMA quiescence.
Recovery Runtime v1.0 adds 250-µs recovery-core reset-status polling to v0.9, preserving reset-first DMA fencing and epoch-gated remapping.
Run 48-hour hardware-in-loop fault campaign on Runtime v1.0, suppressing reset interrupts; measure deadlines, stale DMA, partition writes, and recovery.
Runtime v1.0’s 48-hour campaign recorded zero deadline misses, stale DMA, or partition writes; worst suppressed-interrupt recovery was 49 ms.
Approve Recovery Runtime v1.0: 48-hour testing found zero deadline misses, stale writes, or partition corruption; worst recovery was 49 ms.
